archetype.name: Pocket Passer (short-area volume)
archetype.definition: A rhythm thrower working inside Kellen Moore's quick game. He piles up attempts and completions underneath, keeps himself off the turf, and is at his best on the fewer throws he pushes past ten yards.

report.headline: Volume is real and the sacks are fixed, but the efficiency hasn't followed
report.take:
Shough's surface line looks like a passer on the rise. He's ninth in passing yards, seventh in touchdowns and on a 4,180-yard, 32-TD pace. The efficiency tells a smaller story. His 6.3 yards per attempt ranks 34th of 45, his 0.018 EPA per dropback sits 25th and below the league's 0.04, and his CPOE is slightly negative. The yardage comes from 39 attempts a game on a 2-5 team whose defense ranks 26th, not from each throw being worth much. Compared with his 2025 rookie year, the per-throw value has dropped by about a yard per attempt even as the touchdowns jumped.

What drives the season is a split in how he's used. On throws of ten-plus air yards he's been genuinely good: 0.349 EPA per play, 0.376 on intermediate throws, with Chris Olave turning 71 targets into 0.528 EPA apiece. He just doesn't throw there much. His intended air yards land short of the sticks on average, and the 45 throws behind the line of scrimmage have lost 19.6 EPA, more than wiping out the gain from his entire short game. Week 7 against Pittsburgh showed the ceiling of the dink approach when it's sharp: 30 of 38, +10.6 EPA, with intended air yards of just 4.7. Week 5 against Minnesota, the top-ranked defense, showed the floor: 96 yards, two picks, -11.9 EPA.

Two things in the line deserve skepticism. Eleven of his 13 TD passes came in the red zone, on a 10.1 CPOE there. That is a hot, small-sample number, and it is propping up his touchdown rate while his yards per attempt sinks. On the other side, the turnovers are a real problem. Six interceptions plus three lost fumbles (42nd of 45) and six fumbles charted as turnover-worthy. The interception rate is only league average, so the fumbles are the bigger leak.

The genuine growth is in the pocket. His pressure-to-sack rate was 41.9% as a rookie, 48th of 62. It's 23.6% now, and his sack rate of 5.2% beats the league's 6.7. That looks like a learned skill rather than luck, and it's the piece most likely to stick.

strengths.title: Efficient when he pushes it
strengths.body: On throws of ten-plus air yards he has produced 0.349 EPA per play, and the intermediate band is even better, while the under-10 throws barely clear zero. Olave and Devaughn Vele are both well above 0.4 EPA per target, so he has receivers who win downfield. The skill looks real. The question is whether Moore lets him use it more often, since his aggressiveness is up from his rookie year but the target depth remains short.

strengths.title: Pressure no longer becomes sacks
strengths.body: As a rookie, pressure turned into a sack at one of the worst rates in the league. This year that rate has roughly halved, and his sack rate sits comfortably better than average. With his time to throw basically unchanged from last year, this reads as faster recognition and getting rid of the ball, not a scheme crutch. That kind of improvement usually holds.

strengths.title: Red-zone finishing
strengths.body: He has thrown 11 touchdowns inside the 20 on 35 attempts, completing passes far above expectation. Most of his TD total runs through this split. It's a legitimate positive, but it rests on a small sample and a CPOE he won't keep, so expect the TD rate to drift back toward his yardage efficiency.

concerns.title: Screens and quick game bleed points
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have lost 19.6 EPA with a 26.7% success rate, and his air yards land short of the sticks on average. Part of this is Moore's design and a run game ranked 24th that can't carry the offense. But he is also completing those throws well below expectation, so execution shares the blame. It is why his yards per attempt is about a yard below last season.

concerns.title: Ball security, especially fumbles
concerns.body: Three lost fumbles rank 42nd of 45, and six fumbles were charted as turnover-worthy, so this isn't just bad bounces. The interception rate is merely league average. The fumbling is a flaw in how he holds the ball in the pocket and on the move, and it has already cost a game-sized chunk of value.

concerns.title: Third down and accuracy slide
concerns.body: On third down he is at -0.173 EPA per play, with an average 8.4 yards to go, and six of his sacks came there. Over the last three games his CPOE has fallen to -7.3, including a -17.2 game against the Giants. Long third downs are partly an offense-wide early-down problem. Still, the recent accuracy dip is his, and it needs to reverse.

trend.note: He swings between his best and worst games, with nothing in between. There are two +10 EPA games (Baltimore and Pittsburgh) and a -11.9 against Minnesota. The last five games average negative passing EPA even with the strong Week 7, so the underlying direction is soft rather than improving.

nextGame.headline: Rested, but facing a top-ten pass defense that gets home
nextGame.body:
Cleveland is the second top-ten defense in three games. It ranks sixth in pass EPA allowed, sixth in hit rate and sixth in sack rate, and holds quarterbacks to the eighth-fewest PPR points. That front tests the pocket skill he's built, and it tests his ball security, which is the weakest part of his game. The opening is how Cleveland gets beaten: by third receivers and on the ground. WR3s score well above their norms against the Browns, and the defense is a mild run funnel, allowing the most explosive runs in the league. Cleveland's offense ranks 24th, which may keep the score close and spare him the catch-up passing that has fed his volume.

The Saints come off a 14-day rest. Guard Cesar Ruiz, a 90%-snap starter, is out with a return date estimated for this game; if he's back, it matters against this pass rush. Rookie WR Jordyn Tyson (IR, hamstring) is "getting closer" with the same estimated return. He is the swing piece: Bryce Lance has lost 13.1 EPA on 23 targets, and Tyson taking that WR3 role is exactly where Cleveland is soft. For the Browns, CB Myles Harden (63% of snaps) left Week 7's game questionable with a hamstring, and DT Mike Hall Jr. was out but is expected back before this game. No line is posted yet.

keyMatchups.title: Browns' pass rush vs his pocket
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland generates hits and sacks at a top-six rate. His improved pressure-to-sack rate has kept him upright so far, but Minnesota's elite defense produced his worst game. Whether Ruiz returns at guard shapes how clean the pocket is.

keyMatchups.title: Third receiver is the soft spot
keyMatchups.body: WR3s outscore their averages against Cleveland by more than almost anywhere else, while tight ends are nearly shut down. That points his volume toward Olave and whoever plays the third spot rather than Juwan Johnson. Tyson's return would turn this from a hint into a real edge.

keyMatchups.title: Game script may cap volume
keyMatchups.body: Cleveland's offense is bottom-ten by EPA and its line allows hits at nearly the league's worst rate. A low-scoring, close game is the likely shape. That trims the attempt count his yardage depends on.

nextGame.watch: Whether Moore lets him throw past ten yards more against a defense that's beatable deep but punishing underneath, and whether Tyson is active.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume should keep coming. The Saints pass a bit more than situation predicts and their defense will keep putting them in shootouts, so yardage in the 200s is a fair baseline. The sack avoidance looks real and should hold. What regresses is the red-zone touchdown rate. Without it, his TD output drifts down toward what roughly 6 yards per attempt supports, unless the play-calling lets him live more at the intermediate level, where he's been efficient.

The upside path is Tyson returning to replace Lance's negative targets, along with a modest shift away from screens. The downside is that the fumbling persists and the recent accuracy slide proves real rather than a one-off. Expect a starter-level but below-average efficiency passer whose fantasy line outpaces his real-football value.
swingFactors: Jordyn Tyson's return replacing Bryce Lance's targets
Share of throws beyond ten air yards vs. screens

confidence.note: Seven starts with a stable role, but wild game-to-game swings and a small, hot red-zone sample.
